presentingComplaint: Sudden-onset breathlessness and right-sided pleuritic chest pain since this morning.
history: Previously well 58-year-old woman with acute onset dyspnoea and pleuritic right chest pain for 6 hours, associated with a dry cough. Returned 4 days ago from a 10-hour long-haul flight. Three weeks ago had a right knee arthroscopy with reduced mobility since. On combined oral contraceptive pill. Reports mild right calf discomfort and swelling over the last 2 days. No haemoptysis, no fever. No prior VTE. Ex-smoker (15 pack-years).
examination: Comfortable at rest but tachypnoeic on minimal exertion. Chest clear on auscultation with no focal crepitations or consolidation. Right calf is mildly swollen with tenderness over the deep veins and a positive measurement asymmetry (>3 cm vs left). Loud P2 audible. No signs of overt right heart failure, JVP not grossly elevated. Afebrile. No leg cellulitis or erythema.

labs.ABG: pO2 8.9 kPa, pCO2 4.0 kPa (mild hypoxaemia with respiratory alkalosis)

imaging: CT pulmonary angiogram: filling defects in the right lower lobe segmental and subsegmental pulmonary arteries; no RV:LV ratio >1.0, no evidence of right heart strain. CXR clear (no consolidation, no effusion). ECG: sinus tachycardia; classic S1Q3T3 pattern present. Compression ultrasound right leg confirms popliteal DVT.
finalDiagnosis: Acute pulmonary embolism (intermediate-low risk / haemodynamically stable), provoked by recent surgery, immobility, long-haul travel and combined oral contraceptive use.
citations: Harrison 22e - Deep Venous Thrombosis and Pulmonary Thromboembolism
stewardship: not applicable - non-infective. No antibiotics indicated; management is therapeutic anticoagulation.
contraindications: Assess bleeding risk before anticoagulation; recent surgery raises haemorrhage concern
DOACs require dose adjustment / caution in significant renal impairment (check CrCl)
Avoid CTPA contrast if severe contrast allergy or AKI - consider V/Q scan
edgeCases: Haemodynamically unstable (massive) PE with hypotension warrants systemic thrombolysis rather than anticoagulation alone
A normal D-dimer with low Wells score can safely exclude PE without imaging (PERC/age-adjusted D-dimer), avoiding unnecessary CTPA
PE can present with syncope or isolated tachycardia and a clear chest, mimicking other causes
expectedMaiK: This is a classic provoked pulmonary embolism: sudden pleuritic dyspnoea with hypoxia, tachycardia, an ipsilateral DVT and multiple VTE risk factors (recent surgery, immobility, long-haul flight, oestrogen). Risk-stratify (haemodynamically stable = not high-risk) and start therapeutic anticoagulation promptly while confirming with CTPA.
expectedNextQuestions: Any haemodynamic instability, syncope or hypotension suggesting high-risk (massive) PE?
Any bleeding risk factors or contraindications to anticoagulation (recent surgery, active bleeding)?
Is there unilateral leg swelling/pain suggesting a source DVT?
expectedInvestigations: Age-adjusted D-dimer with Wells score risk stratification
ECG and troponin/BNP for right heart strain assessment
regressionAssertions: differential must not label this as an infective pneumonia as the primary diagnosis
